agent.problem: This non-opening story card has three punctuated sentence units: 'Then a noise.', the description of the tumult and uproar, and the battery joke. Story cards after the opening are limited to one or two sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

agent.problem: The story card says the invaders are coming 'to destroy the whole country,' immediately before card 9 asks what the Day of the LORD will come as, with 'destruction' as the answer. Saying 'destroy' hands the baker the answer rather than leaving the choice meaningful.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

agent.problem: The phrase 'these terrified people' has no antecedent within the question and points back to the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to establish the moment itself, such as the terror and anguish accompanying the Day of the LORD.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

agent.problem: This non-opening story card has three punctuated sentence units: the statement about gold, 'Not just any gold, the gold of Ophir.', and the 25-cent joke. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

agent.problem: The card reduces Isaiah 13:16 to 'families suffer terribly,' never telling the baker that infants are dashed to pieces before their eyes and wives are ravished. It also drops the stabbing from verse 15. These omissions leave out the substance of the cited verses, not merely incidental detail.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

agent.problem: This choice card itself introduces both the Medes and God's stirring them up against Babylon, while the preceding story card covers verses 15-16. The setup for this new moment in verse 17 should be told on a story card rather than packed into the question.

rule.text: The setup for a choice is on a story card.

human.problem: Isaiah 13:16 describes infants dashed to pieces and wives ravished. The card says 'families suffer terribly,' right after saying 'Isaiah doesn't soften this part.' So the card softens the text while saying the text isn't softened. The docs say the content is for adults and must be 'always clean,' and that things are called what the text calls them, but they don't say how to handle graphic violence or sexual violence in Scripture.
human.question: For graphic violence or sexual violence in a passage, like Isaiah 13:16, should Prep name what the text says, use a gentler summary, or leave it to the reveal screen? If it uses a summary, should the lead-in line ('doesn't soften this part') be dropped?

human.problem: Many story cards tell this future-tense prophecy in the present tense: 'Terror, pain and anguish seize them,' 'The heavens tremble,' 'Hyenas howl in her fortresses.' That can make a prophecy sound like something happening now or already done. The docs don't say what tense to use when retelling prophecy.
human.question: When Prep retells a prophecy written in the future tense ('will'), may Papa Dorin tell it in the present tense like a story, or should he keep the future tense ('will')?

human.problem: Isaiah 13:16 says infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes and wives will be ravished. The card sums this up as 'families suffer terribly,' right after saying 'Isaiah doesn't soften this part.' The card softens it while saying it doesn't. The docs say to call things what the text calls them and not to stretch the text, but they don't say how to handle graphic violence for an adult audience that kids may also play.
human.question: How plainly should Prep retell graphic violence like Isaiah 13:16? Should it name what the text says, use a gentler summary, or leave the detail out? If a gentler summary is allowed, should the card drop lines like 'Isaiah doesn't soften this part'?
